docs.title: GReMS
docs.text:
Graph-Reinforced Neural Micro-Splitting over Dynamic Heterogeneous IoT Networks

GReMS is a PPO based reinforcement learning agent that optimises split inference of VGG-16 over wireless networks of heterogeneous IoT and edge devices. For each inference request the agent decides:

  • where to cut the network into sequential pipeline stages (vertical split),
  • how many workers run each stage in parallel (horizontal split),
  • which node is the hub that distributes the input and routes data,
  • which physical node takes each worker role.

The objective is low end to end latency under changing node load and link bandwidth. One trained policy covers topologies with 3 to 20 nodes, including sizes never seen during training. GReMS is compared with the DiSNet, MoDNN and EnSplit baselines.

docs.title: Project at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    A[Topology generator] --> B[SplitEnv]
    C[MMPP load and Gilbert-Elliott bandwidth] --> B
    B -->|542 dim observation| D[GNN actor critic]
    D -->|split plan| B
    B -->|latency model| E[reward]
    E --> F[PPO update]
    F --> D

The environment samples a network, advances the channel state, asks the agent for a split plan, estimates the resulting latency with an analytical model calibrated on a Jetson Nano and returns -5 * log(latency_ms) plus shaped penalties as reward.

docs.title: Code structure
docs.text: The Python modules live flat in the repository root (they import each other by plain module name, for example from config import ...), so run every script from the repository root.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
GReMS/
├── scripts/                 Reproducible entry points (shell) and result summariser
├── docs/, mkdocs.yml        This documentation
├── checkpoints/             Released weights and learning curves
├── data/
│   ├── networks/            Compressed topology archives (train and test graphs)
│   ├── offline_profiles/    layer_profiles.json, used with --offline
│   └── baselines.json       Original DiSNet testbed reference numbers (not used by the code)
├── third_party/disnet/      Vendored DiSNet code for the DiSNet and MoDNN baselines
└── *.py                     Core code, see below

Directories created at run time and not tracked by git: variable_networks*/ (extracted topologies), results/ (evaluation JSON), plots/, logs/.

Several values are overridable by environment variables. GNNActorCritic, build_model reward.py -ALPHA * log(latency_ms). compute_reward run_rl_live.py Analytical latency model for a GReMS plan, including multi hop routing. measure_rl_plan_latency_ms profiling.py Layer profiles, and conversion of a NetworkX topology into node and link profiles. generate_profiles_from_disnet_graph, load_layer_profiles generate_variable_networks.py Random topology generator and path helper. generate_all, get_variable_network_paths utils.py Logging, seeding, JSON helpers. set_seed, setup_logging

docs.title: Training and evaluation
docs.text: File Role train_GReMS.py PPO training loop with GAE, reward normalisation, curriculum, resume and optional W&B. Entry point: python train_GReMS.py --help. evaluate_GReMS.py Dynamic multi sequence evaluator. Runs GReMS and the baselines on the same channel trajectories and writes a JSON per run.

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text: File Role run_disnet_live.py DiSNet plan and latency under the shared latency tables run_modnn_live.py MoDNN plan and latency run_ensplit_live.py EnSplit (brute force or DDQN) ensplit_ddqn.py, ensplit_env.py, train_ensplit.py EnSplit DDQN agent, environment and training script third_party/disnet/ Original DiSNet functions used by the first two

docs.title: Data flow in one training step
docs.text:
1. train_GReMS.py samples an environment from the pool (a SplitEnv bound to one topology file).
  2. SplitEnv.reset() advances ComputeLoadModel and LinkBWModel and builds node and link profiles via profiling.py.
  3. state_encoder.encode_state() produces the 542 dimensional observation.
  4. GNNActorCritic.act() samples an action, action_space.decode_action() turns it into a plan.
  5. run_rl_live.measure_rl_plan_latency_ms() returns the latency, reward.compute_reward() and the penalties in environment.py return the reward.
  6. After 512 steps ppo_update() runs 4 epochs of clipped PPO.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Latency is in milliseconds, bandwidth in Mbit/s in topology files and MB/s inside the latency model.
  • A "group" is a vertical stage. A "chunk" is a horizontal slice of one group. A "worker" is a node that runs one chunk.
  • Node indices are 0 based and refer to the NetworkX graph. Padded nodes have index at least N.
  • Plans are dictionaries with keys group_sizes, chunks, hub_node, assignment.

docs.title: Configuration reference
docs.text: Most constants live in config.py. A subset can be overridden with environment variables without editing code. The defaults are the paper settings.

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Default (paper value) Meaning GE_TRANS_GB 0.15 P(GOOD to BAD) of the link chain GE_TRANS_BG 0.40 P(BAD to GOOD) GE_BW_GOOD_FACTOR_MIN/MAX 0.80 / 1.00 bandwidth fraction in GOOD state GE_BW_BAD_FACTOR_MIN/MAX 0.15 / 0.25 bandwidth fraction in BAD state NODE_UTIL_BONUS 0.0 reward bonus for using more nodes (disabled) CONN_PENALTY_START 5.0 (Stage 2 uses 50.0, set by its script) start of the connectivity penalty ramp VARIABLE_TRAIN_SIZES 3,...,20 (the stage scripts set 4,...,10 and 4,...,20) node counts sampled in training WEAK_LINK_BW_THRESHOLD 2.0 MB/s below which a first hop link is penalised WEAK_LINK_PENALTY_BETA 10.0 weight of that penalty ENTROPY_COEFF_END 0.002 final entropy coefficient ENTROPY_DECAY_STEPS 2 000 000 steps over which entropy decays VALUE_COEFF 0.5 critic loss weight REWARD_RMS_RESUME_COUNT_CAP 0 (off) caps the reward normaliser count on resume

docs.title: Constants in config.py
docs.text:
Group Names Notes Model MODEL_CFG, NUM_LAYERS = 21, LAYER_KERNEL_CFG, LAYER_SPATIAL_OUT VGG-16 definition with FLOPs and activation sizes Timing LAYER_FWD_MS, LAYER_IOT_FWD_MS, IOT_REF_WEIGHT, DEVICE_SCALING_DIMINISHING_RETURN Xeon timings scaled to a Jetson Nano Network MAX_NODES = 20, DISNET_BW_CAP = 200, BW_NORM_SCALE padding size and bandwidth normalisation Channels MMPP_*, COMPUTE_SLOWDOWN_MAX, GE_*, EPISODE_LENGTH = 10 see Problem and environment Action space MAX_GROUPS = 6, MAX_CHUNKS = MAX_NODES, N_VERT_WEIGHTS = 8 sizes of the action heads Reward ALPHA = 5, CONNECTIVITY_PENALTY_BETA, CONN_PENALTY_END = 50, CONN_PENALTY_WARMUP_STEPS = 500000, SINGLE_NODE_PENALTY = 140, MEMORY_OVERLOAD_PENALTY = 200, ROUTING_QUALITY_BONUS = 5 see Reward and training PPO PPO_LR, PPO_GAMMA, PPO_GAE_LAMBDA, PPO_CLIP_EPS, PPO_EPOCHS, PPO_BATCH_SIZE, NUM_ROLLOUT_STEPS, PPO_MAX_GRAD_NORM command line flags override the learning rate, batch size, clip and entropy Overheads OVERHEAD_REMOTE_NODE_SETUP = 5 ms, OVERHEAD_PER_CHUNK = 1.5 ms, OVERHEAD_PER_DATA_TRANSFER = 0.5 ms added to the latency model Paths PROJECT_ROOT, DATA_DIR, CHECKPOINT_DIR, LOG_DIR derived from the location of config.py

Importing config creates data/offline_profiles/, checkpoints/ and logs/ if they are missing.

Changing a constant changes the problem

The released checkpoints were trained for one observation layout (542 dimensions), one action layout and one latency model. Changing MAX_NODES, MAX_GROUPS, MAX_CHUNKS, N_VERT_WEIGHTS or anything that alters the observation size makes the released weights incompatible. Changing penalties, channel parameters or timings keeps them loadable but results will no longer match the paper.

docs.title: Main evaluation (evaluate_GReMS.py)
docs.text:
Output: one JSON per seed, results/<RUN_ID>_<topology>[_s<seed>].json. The files can be large (hundreds of MB for a full 3 to 20 node sweep) because they store every step of every trajectory.

Structure:

Key Content run_id, topology_tag, model_path, num_sequences, num_steps, obs_dim run description networks.<name>.sequences[i].steps[t] per step latencies rl_lat_ms, frozen_lat_ms, disnet_lat_ms, modnn_lat_ms, ensplit_lat_ms, channel statistics (mean_load, frac_high, node_loads, link_bws_mbit), plan (hub_node, worker_nodes) and connected size_summary.<N> per node count: rl_mean, rl_std, disnet_mean, modnn_mean, ensplit_mean, connectivity rate, win rates rl_beat_* step_curves latency as a function of the step index, averaged over networks

frozen_lat_ms is the latency of the plan chosen at step 0 and kept while the channel changes. It shows the value of adapting. connected is false if the plan uses a missing link. rl_mean_conn and the *_conn fields restrict the statistics to connected plans.

Aggregate seeds with scripts/summarize_results.py.

docs.title: Generalisation to other topology families
docs.text:
The same checkpoint is evaluated on WS, ER and BA test networks without any retraining:

for t in ws er ba; do bash scripts/evaluate.sh checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt $t; done

Extra BA test sets with different attachment parameters m = 1, 3, 4 are in data/networks/variable_networks_ba_m{1,3,4}.tar.gz (test networks only). Evaluate them with --networks-dir variable_networks_ba_m1 --topology-tag ba in evaluate_GReMS.py.

docs.title: EnSplit baseline (train_ensplit.py)
docs.text: Output: checkpoints/ensplit/ensplit_best.pt, ensplit_final.pt and learning_curve.csv.

docs.title: Extending GReMS
docs.text: This page lists the usual extension points and the files to touch. Always re-run the smoke test of the Quick start after a change.

docs.title: Use a different DNN than VGG-16
docs.text:
1. Describe the model in config.py: replace MODEL_CFG, LAYER_FWD_MS, LAYER_KERNEL_CFG and LAYER_SPATIAL_OUT. NUM_LAYERS follows from MODEL_CFG.
  2. Check state_encoder.py (blocks 4 and 8 depend on the number of layers, so state_dim() changes) and action_space.py (the vertical weight decoder).
  3. run_rl_live.py assumes a layer sequence of spatial layers followed by fully connected layers. Other topologies (residual connections) need a new dependency DAG.
  4. The baselines hard code VGG-16 layer ranges (run_disnet_live.py, run_modnn_live.py). Update or disable them.
  5. Retrain from scratch. Checkpoints are not transferable.

docs.title: Change the reward
docs.text: Edit reward.py for the main term and the shaping block in SplitEnv.step() (environment.py). Penalty magnitudes are in config.py. When the scale of the reward changes keep the online normaliser in train_GReMS.py (RunningMeanStd).

docs.title: Add a channel model
docs.text: network_dynamics.py contains the two models behind a small interface (advance(), getters for load or bandwidth, resize()). Implement the same methods in a new class and instantiate it in SplitEnv.__init__ and SplitEnv.reset(). The observation already contains the effective load and bandwidth, so no encoder change is needed unless you add new state variables.

docs.title: Add a topology family
docs.text: Add a generator in generate_variable_networks.py (see _make_ba_graph and the others), register its name in SUPPORTED_TOPOLOGY_MODELS, generate files with --topology-model <name>, and add the directory to the maps _dir_map in evaluate_GReMS.py and _topo_dir_map in train_GReMS.py. Each node needs a weight attribute and each edge a weight (bandwidth), as in the existing files.

docs.title: Add a baseline
docs.text: Create run_<name>_live.py with a function that takes a NetworkX graph with the same attributes and returns a dictionary with latency_ms. Call it from evaluate_one_network in evaluate_GReMS.py next to the existing baselines and add its latency to the step record and to _aggregate_by_size.

docs.title: Plug in a real latency measurement
docs.text: measure_rl_plan_latency_ms in run_rl_live.py takes a plan plus node and link state and returns a latency. Replacing it by lookups from measurements on your hardware is the easiest way to calibrate to a new testbed. Keep the signature and the plan keys unchanged and everything else works.

docs.title: Change the network architecture
docs.text: gnn_model.py defines PhysicalNetworkGNN (the backbone) and GNNActorCritic (heads). build_model is the single construction point used by training and evaluation. If you change the parameter shapes, old checkpoints will not load.

docs.title: Coding conventions
docs.text:
• Python modules stay flat in the root, imports are plain (from config import X).
  • Constants go to config.py, tunable ones read an environment variable.
  • New experiments get a script in scripts/ that sources _common.sh and writes to results/.
  • Document new settings in Configuration reference and new commands in Scripts reference.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Linux or macOS (developed on Debian 12, Python 3.11).
  • Python 3.9 or newer. The released results were produced with Python 3.11.
  • About 1 GB of disk space (most of it is the checkpoints).
  • A GPU is only needed for re-training. Evaluation, the demo and all baselines run on CPU.
Package Tested version Used for torch 2.10 actor critic, EnSplit DDQN gymnasium 1.2 environment interface numpy 2.4 everything networkx 3.6 topologies and routing matplotlib 3.10 topology plots and the demo wandb 0.25 (optional) training curves when --wandb-project is given

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
git clone <repository-url> GReMS
cd GReMS

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

If you use conda:

conda create -n grems python=3.11 -y
conda activate grems
pip install -r requirements.txt

On a GPU machine install the PyTorch build that matches your CUDA version first, following https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/, then run pip install -r requirements.txt.

docs.title: Unpack the network topologies
docs.text:
The train and test topologies are stored as small compressed archives in data/networks/. Extract them once:

bash scripts/setup_networks.sh            # all families
bash scripts/setup_networks.sh rgg        # only random geometric graphs

This creates variable_networks_rgg/, variable_networks_ws/, variable_networks_er/, variable_networks/ (Barabasi-Albert, m = 2) and the test only sets variable_networks_ba_m1/, _m3/, _m4/ next to the code.

Do not regenerate the topologies if you want paper numbers

generate_variable_networks.py is seeded, but the shipped networks were created by earlier revisions of the generator. Regenerating gives different graphs and therefore slightly different numbers. Use the archives for reproduction and the generator only for new experiments.

docs.title: Check the installation
docs.text:
python -c "import torch, gymnasium, networkx; print(torch.__version__, gymnasium.__version__, networkx.__version__)"
python -c "import config; print(config.MAX_NODES, config.NUM_LAYERS)"      # prints: 20 21

Then continue with the Quick start.

docs.text:
pip install -r requirements-docs.txt
mkdocs serve        # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build        # static site in site/

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: All commands are run from the repository root with the environment from Installation active.

docs.title: 1. Evaluate the released model on a few networks
docs.text:
SEEDS="0" SIZES=small BASELINES=1 NUM_SEQ=1 NUM_STEPS=5 bash scripts/evaluate.sh

What this does:

  • loads checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt,
  • evaluates it on the held out RGG test networks with 3 to 10 nodes (10 networks per size),
  • runs DiSNet, MoDNN and EnSplit on exactly the same channel states,
  • writes results/GReMS_Final_Finetune_rgg.json.

Summarise the output:

python scripts/summarize_results.py results/GReMS_Final_Finetune_rgg.json

Example (shortened, one trajectory so numbers are noisy):

 N  GReMS (ms)  DiSNet (ms)  MoDNN (ms)  EnSplit (ms)
--  ----------  -----------  ----------  ------------
 4        2782         8256       29265          4074
 6        2314         6927       11084          3061
10        2056         5879       26788          4146

docs.title: 2. Train a tiny model (smoke test)
docs.text:
DEVICE=cpu TIMESTEPS=20480 RUN_ID=smoke bash scripts/train_stage1.sh

This checks that training, checkpointing and logging work. Expect 10 to 30 minutes on a CPU machine, because 350 training environments are built first and every PPO update simulates 512 steps. It is a plumbing test and the resulting policy is meaningless. The checkpoint appears in checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_smoke/. The real run uses 30 million steps, see the Reproducibility guide.

docs.title: 3. Load the policy in your own code
docs.text:
import torch
from config import MAX_NODES
from environment import SplitEnv
from gnn_model import build_model

env = SplitEnv(num_nodes=MAX_NODES, use_offline_profiles=False, seed=0)
obs_dim = env.observation_space.shape[0]            # 542

path = "checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt"
raw = torch.load(path, map_location="cpu", weights_only=False)
policy = build_model(obs_dim, env.spec_action)
policy.load_state_dict(raw["model"] if "model" in raw else raw)
policy.eval()

evaluate_one_network in evaluate_GReMS.py shows how a topology file is turned into an environment, how observations are encoded and how the policy output is decoded into a plan. It is the best starting point for embedding the policy in another system.

docs.title: Overview of the pipeline
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    N[data/networks archives] -->|setup_networks.sh| T[variable_networks_rgg etc.]
    T --> S1[Stage 1: train_stage1.sh<br/>N = 4 to 10, 30M steps]
    S1 -->|grems_final.pt| S2[Stage 2: train_finetune.sh<br/>N = 4 to 20, 10M steps]
    S2 -->|grems_final.pt| E[evaluate.sh<br/>5 seeds]
    P[released checkpoints] --> E
    E -->|results/*.json| R[summarize_results.py]

You can enter the pipeline at any point. Evaluating the released checkpoints (Level 1) is the fastest way to audit the reported numbers. Re-training (Level 2) checks that the training recipe produces an equivalent policy.

Level What you reproduce Hardware Wall clock 0. Smoke test The code runs end to end CPU minutes 1. Evaluation Latency tables from the released checkpoints CPU, 8+ cores hours 2. Training The checkpoints themselves 1 GPU (16 GB used for the release) about 2 days for Stage 1, about 16 hours for Stage 2 3. Extra experiments EnSplit baseline retraining, other topology families CPU hours

docs.title: Step 0. The settings that matter
docs.text:
The defaults in config.py are the settings of every reported result, so no environment variables are needed for the main experiments. The two training stages differ only in the values below, which scripts/train_stage1.sh and scripts/train_finetune.sh set for you.

Setting Value Link chain, P(GOOD to BAD) / P(BAD to GOOD) 0.15 / 0.40 Bandwidth factor in BAD / GOOD state 0.15 to 0.25 / 0.80 to 1.00 of base Compute load (MMPP) LOW 0.10 to 0.35, HIGH 0.55 to 0.80, P(LOW to HIGH) = 0.05, P(HIGH to LOW) = 0.20 NODE_UTIL_BONUS 0.0 Reward scale ALPHA 5 VARIABLE_TRAIN_SIZES Stage 1: 4 to 10, Stage 2: 4 to 20 (set by the scripts) CONN_PENALTY_START Stage 1: 5.0 (default), Stage 2: 50.0 (set by the script)

If you change any of these in config.py or through an environment variable of the same name, you are no longer reproducing the paper. The full list of knobs is in the Configuration reference.

docs.title: Step 1. Environment and data
docs.text:
pip install -r requirements.txt
bash scripts/setup_networks.sh

The archives contain, per topology family, 50 training and 10 test networks for every size from 3 to 20 nodes. Test networks are the files named varnet_<N>nodes_test_<i>.txt. Training never sees them.

docs.title: Step 2. Level 1: evaluate the released checkpoints
docs.text:
# GReMS only, 5 seeds, all sizes (3 to 20), RGG topologies
bash scripts/evaluate.sh

# Same, but also run DiSNet, MoDNN and EnSplit on identical channel states
BASELINES=1 bash scripts/evaluate.sh

# Other topology families (generalisation, the model never trained on them)
bash scripts/evaluate.sh checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt ws
bash scripts/evaluate.sh checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt er
bash scripts/evaluate.sh checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt ba

# Aggregate the 5 seeds
python scripts/summarize_results.py results/GReMS_Final_Finetune_rgg*.json

The evaluation protocol is fixed in the script:

  • 10 held out networks per node count, node counts 3 to 20,
  • 10 independent trajectories per network, 50 steps each,
  • at every step the compute load (MMPP) and every link (Gilbert-Elliott) advance, and all methods are evaluated on the same state,
  • seeds 0, 100, 200, 300, 400,
  • reported number per node count: mean latency over networks, then mean and standard deviation over seeds.

Use --num-sequences, --num-steps and SEEDS only for quick checks. Changing them changes the numbers.

To evaluate the Stage 1 checkpoint instead:

bash scripts/evaluate.sh checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_FINAL/grems_final.pt rgg GReMS_FINAL

docs.title: Reference numbers from the authors' runs
docs.text:
Mean latency in ms of GReMS (fine tuned model, RGG test networks), mean ± std over the 5 seeds 0, 100, 200, 300, 400. These come from the authors' own earlier evaluation runs (GReMS only, --no-baselines) and were not re-run when this documentation was written. A full re-run takes hours, so treat the table as an orientation, and expect small deviations from hardware and library versions.

N GReMS (ms) N GReMS (ms) N GReMS (ms) 3 3950 ± 89 9 2730 ± 52 15 2492 ± 49 4 3130 ± 77 10 2416 ± 45 16 2440 ± 22 5 3088 ± 103 11 2523 ± 20 17 2452 ± 59 6 2804 ± 49 12 2485 ± 41 18 2534 ± 32 7 3154 ± 36 13 2396 ± 23 19 2273 ± 41 8 2611 ± 41 14 2671 ± 56 20 2495 ± 18
  • GReMS has lower mean latency than DiSNet and MoDNN on nearly every test network, and lower than EnSplit on most networks, for all sizes 3 to 20. The GReMS beats X on k/n networks lines in the log and the rl_beat_* fields in the JSON give the exact counts.
  • Absolute latencies are in the low seconds for 3 to 10 nodes. MoDNN is often an order of magnitude slower because it keeps all fully connected layers on the hub.
  • Across seeds the per size mean varies by a few percent. A single seed is not enough to judge a difference smaller than that, use all five.
  • If your numbers do not match, first check that no GE_*, NODE_UTIL_BONUS or VARIABLE_TRAIN_SIZES variable is set in your shell.

docs.title: Sources of non determinism
docs.text: Source Effect Mitigation Seeds Evaluation draws channel trajectories from a seeded generator, so a fixed seed on the same machine repeats exactly Use the seeds listed above PyTorch version and CPU/GPU Floating point differences can flip an argmax between two near equal actions Use CPU for evaluation, expect rare single step differences that average out Baseline time limits DiSNet and MoDNN have a per step wall clock limit (30 s for N up to 10, 10 s for N from 11, set by _BASELINE_TIMEOUT_S and _OOD_BASELINE_TIMEOUT_S in evaluate_GReMS.py). On a very slow machine a baseline can time out and is then excluded from that network Run on a machine with 8 or more free cores. Check for timeout messages in the log Topology files Different graphs give different numbers Use the archives in data/networks/, never regenerate

docs.title: Stage 1, from scratch on N = 4 to 10
docs.text:
DEVICE=cuda bash scripts/train_stage1.sh

Equivalent explicit command (after export VARIABLE_TRAIN_SIZES=4,5,6,7,8,9,10):

python train_GReMS.py --run-id GReMS_FINAL --variable-networks --topology-models rgg \
    --timesteps 30000000 --rollout 512 --batch-size 512 --lr 3e-4 \
    --entropy-coeff 0.02 --clip-eps 0.2 --eval-interval 200000 --offline --device cuda \
    --best-model-path  checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_FINAL/grems_best.pt \
    --final-model-path checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_FINAL/grems_final.pt

Why checkpoints end up in checkpoints/checkpoints/

train_GReMS.py prepends CHECKPOINT_DIR (checkpoints/) to the given paths, so checkpoints/variable_networks_X/ becomes checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_X/. The scripts and the released layout keep this convention.

Facts about the run:

  • The training pool holds one environment per training network (50 per size, 350 for N = 4 to 10). Each PPO update uses a rollout of 512 steps sampled across that pool, so 30 million steps are about 58 600 updates of 4 epochs each.
  • The learning rate is annealed linearly to zero, the entropy coefficient decays from 0.02 to 0.002 over the first 2 million steps, the connectivity penalty ramps from 5 to 50 over 500k steps.
  • Every 200k steps the policy is evaluated on a fixed set of held out networks and learning_curve.csv is appended. The best model by this metric is stored as grems_best.pt.
  • grems_latest.pt is written every 50 rollouts. Re-running the same command resumes from it automatically after an interruption.

Compare your learning curve with the released one:

import pandas as pd
ref = pd.read_csv("checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_FINAL/learning_curve.csv")
new = pd.read_csv("checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_FINAL_repro/learning_curve.csv")
print(ref[["step", "seen_lat_ms_rgg"]].tail(), new[["step", "seen_lat_ms_rgg"]].tail())

(pandas is not in requirements.txt, install it only if you want this snippet.)

docs.title: Stage 2, fine tune to N = 4 to 20
docs.text:
DEVICE=cuda bash scripts/train_finetune.sh

It loads grems_final.pt of Stage 1, resets the learning rate schedule (--resume-step 0), lowers the learning rate to 3e-5, adds the sizes 11 to 20 and samples them with twice the weight (--large-graph-size 11). CONN_PENALTY_START=50 keeps the connectivity penalty at its final value. Restarting the curriculum from 5 makes connectivity violations explode.

To use your own Stage 1 result as the source, pass SOURCE_RUN_ID, for example SOURCE_RUN_ID=GReMS_FINAL_repro RUN_ID=GReMS_Final_Finetune_repro bash scripts/train_finetune.sh.

docs.title: What counts as reproduced
docs.text:
Training uses GPU kernels and a stochastic policy, so two runs with the same seed are not bit identical. A re-training reproduces the paper if

  1. the learning curve follows the released one in shape and ends in a similar latency range, and
  2. the Level 1 evaluation of your checkpoint shows the same ranking against the baselines and per size means within the seed to seed spread of the released checkpoint.

docs.title: Step 4. Level 3: baseline retraining
docs.text:
bash scripts/train_ensplit.sh               # retrain the EnSplit DDQN baseline

See Experiments and outputs for the output formats.

docs.title: Audit checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] python --version, pip freeze recorded
  • [ ] No overriding environment variables set (env | grep -E "GE_|NODE_UTIL|CONN_|VARIABLE_" is empty)
  • [ ] Topologies extracted from data/networks/, not regenerated
  • [ ] Checkpoint path is the released one (compare with md5sum)
  • [ ] 5 seeds, 10 sequences, 50 steps
  • [ ] Baselines evaluated on the same run (BASELINES=1), no timeouts in the log

docs.title: Scripts reference
docs.text:
All scripts live in scripts/, can be started from any directory and change to the repository root themselves. Options are passed as environment variables.

Script Purpose Options setup_networks.sh [topo ...] Extract topology archives from data/networks/ topologies: rgg ws er ba ba_m1 ba_m3 ba_m4 train_stage1.sh Stage 1 training, N = 4 to 10, 30M steps DEVICE (cuda), TIMESTEPS, RUN_ID (GReMS_FINAL), SEED (42) train_finetune.sh Stage 2 fine tuning, N = 4 to 20, 10M steps DEVICE, TIMESTEPS, RUN_ID (GReMS_Final_Finetune), SOURCE_RUN_ID (GReMS_FINAL), SEED evaluate.sh [MODEL] [TOPO] [RUN_ID] Multi seed evaluation SEEDS, BASELINES (0/1), DEVICE, SIZES (small ood large), NUM_SEQ, NUM_STEPS train_ensplit.sh Train the EnSplit DDQN baseline CHECKPOINT_DIR summarize_results.py FILES... Aggregate result JSONs over seeds into a table --csv out.csv

Set PYTHON=/path/to/python to choose the interpreter.

docs.title: Size groups in evaluate.sh
docs.text:
Group Node counts Note small 3 to 10 seen sizes for both checkpoints (3 was never trained on) ood 11 to 19 unseen by the Stage 1 model, trained for the fine tuned model large 20 the largest supported size

The label "ood" refers to the Stage 1 model. For the Stage 2 model these sizes are in the training range, the test networks themselves are still held out.

docs.title: Direct use of the Python entry points
docs.text:
Equivalent explicit command for the most common evaluation:

python evaluate_GReMS.py \
    --model checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_GReMS_Final_Finetune/grems_final.pt \
    --run-id GReMS_Final_Finetune --topology-tag rgg \
    --num-sequences 10 --num-steps 50 --seed 0 --offline --device cpu \
    --save-json results/GReMS_Final_Finetune_rgg.json

python evaluate_GReMS.py --help and python train_GReMS.py --help list every flag. The main ones:

Flag Meaning --topology-tag topology family to evaluate: rgg, ws, er, ba --num-sequences, --num-steps trajectories per network and steps per trajectory --warmup-steps channel advances before recording starts (default 0) --no-baselines, --no-disnet, --no-modnn skip baselines for speed --ensplit-checkpoint use the trained DDQN instead of brute force EnSplit --no-small, --no-ood-size, --no-large skip a size group --networks-dir evaluate on a custom topology folder --offline use data/offline_profiles/layer_profiles.json (the paper runs use it) --resume, --resume-step (train) continue or fine tune from a checkpoint, reset the schedule --large-graph-size, --small-graph-size (train) oversample graphs at least or at most this size --topology-models (train) one or several of rgg ba ws er for mixed topology training

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Cause and fix Networks directory not found: .../variable_networks_rgg Topologies are not extracted. Run bash scripts/setup_networks.sh. Checkpoint not found Wrong path. Released checkpoints are in checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_<run>/ (note the doubled checkpoints). FileNotFoundError for data/offline_profiles/layer_profiles.json The file is needed by --offline (used by the paper scripts) and is tracked in git. Restore it with git checkout data/offline_profiles/layer_profiles.json. ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'networkx' (or torch, gymnasium) Install requirements in the active environment: pip install -r requirements.txt. RuntimeError: ... size mismatch for ... when loading a checkpoint The code constants differ from the ones used for training (MAX_NODES, MAX_GROUPS, observation layout). Use the code revision that matches the checkpoint. torch.load fails with weights_only or pickle errors Checkpoints contain more than tensors. The code passes weights_only=False. Do this only for checkpoints you trust. Evaluation is very slow Baselines dominate the run time, especially DiSNet and MoDNN above 10 nodes. Use BASELINES=0 for GReMS only, or SIZES=small. Messages about baseline timeouts The machine is too slow or busy for the per step limits. Free CPU cores or re-run. The timed out network is evaluated without that baseline. Training: CUDA out of memory Use --device cpu for a smoke test, or reduce --batch-size. The reference runs used a 16 GB GPU. Training restarts from the beginning The checkpoint directory differs between runs. The scripts resume from checkpoints/checkpoints/variable_networks_<RUN_ID>/grems_latest.pt so keep RUN_ID constant. Fine tuning fails with connectivity penalty explosion The curriculum was reset. Set CONN_PENALTY_START=50 as train_finetune.sh does. ImportError about network, utils, inference in a baseline The vendored DiSNet code was removed or moved. Keep third_party/disnet/ intact. MkDocs: mermaid fences are shown as code Use mkdocs-material and keep the pymdownx.superfences block of mkdocs.yml.

If none of this helps, open an issue with the output of python --version, pip freeze, the exact command and the last 50 lines of logs/*.log.

docs.title: The agent
docs.text: The policy is a graph neural network actor critic, implemented in gnn_model.py (GNNActorCritic, about 428k parameters).

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    O[542 dim observation] --> P[_parse_obs]
    P --> G[GraphSAGE x3<br/>128 dim, BW weighted edges]
    P --> M[model encoder MLP<br/>per layer split costs]
    P --> X[global statistics and previous action]
    G --> C[shared context MLP 256]
    M --> C
    X --> C
    C --> H1[num_active_groups]
    C --> H2[vertical_weights]
    C --> H3[horizontal_chunks]
    G --> H4[hub_selection pointer]
    G --> H5[node_assignment pointer network]
    C --> V[value head]
  • GraphSAGE backbone. Three layers over the physical network graph with bandwidth weighted edges. Output: one embedding per node and a mean pooled graph embedding.
  • Model encoder. An MLP over per layer features (activation size, cumulative FLOPs) of the 21 VGG-16 layers.
  • Shared context. Fuses global statistics, the graph embedding, the model embedding and the previous action into a 256 dimensional vector.
  • Padding and masking. The observation always has the same size. Topologies with fewer than 20 nodes are zero padded and the padded nodes receive a logit of minus infinity, so the agent can never choose a ghost node. This is what lets one network serve every size from 3 to 20.

docs.title: Action heads
docs.text:
Head Output Controls num_active_groups categorical, 1 to 6 number of vertical stages vertical_weights 6 categoricals with 8 bins relative number of layers per stage horizontal_chunks 6 categoricals, up to 20 bins parallel workers per stage hub_selection per node score hub node node_assignment pointer network over 6 x 20 slots physical node for each worker slot

action_space.py decodes the raw integers into a plan with keys group_sizes, chunks, hub_node and assignment. The decoder guarantees by construction that workers of the first group are distinct and adjacent to the hub, so connectivity cannot be violated by those workers.

docs.title: Observation (542 dimensions)
docs.text:
Built by state_encoder.encode_state. Blocks 1 to 5 are aggregate statistics and independent of network size. Blocks 6 to 9 are zero padded to 20 nodes.

Block Dims Content 1 node stats 16 mean, std, min, max of compute, load, effective capacity, degree 2 link stats 8 mean, std, min, max of bandwidth and latency 3 topology meta 5 normalised node count, edge density, degree statistics 4 model features 12 cumulative FLOPs and maximum activation per group 5 topology structure 15 clustering, assortativity, path lengths, algebraic connectivity 6 per node features 80 compute, load, effective capacity, degree for 20 nodes 7 path and hub 40 path flag and hub score for 20 nodes 8 layer split costs 42 normalised activation size and cumulative FLOP fraction for 21 layers 9 bottleneck bandwidth 190 pairwise minimum path bandwidth, upper triangle of a 20 x 20 matrix 10 previous action 134 normalised previous action vector

The agent observes the true current channel state (loads and effective bandwidths).

docs.title: Baselines
docs.text:
All baselines are evaluated live. At every evaluation step they see the same compute load and link bandwidth state as GReMS, and their plan is scored with the same latency lookup tables.

Method File Idea DiSNet run_disnet_live.py Four vertical groups (layers [0,4), [4,9), [9,14), [14,18)). Path selection, hub selection (determine_opt_neighbours) and the horizontal split ratio (find_split_ratio) come from the original DiSNet code. MoDNN run_modnn_live.py The hub splits all 18 spatial layers across its neighbours. Fully connected layers run on the hub only. EnSplit run_ensplit_live.py Vertical split only. A chain of 4 nodes is extracted between source and destination, then the best contiguous layer assignment is found. Without a checkpoint it is brute force optimal over at most 969 candidates. With --ensplit-checkpoint a trained DDQN picks the action.

docs.title: DiSNet and MoDNN code
docs.text: The decision functions of the two baselines are the original DiSNet implementation, vendored in third_party/disnet/ (see its README for provenance). run_disnet_live.py and run_modnn_live.py import these modules inside a temporary sys.modules sandbox because the original files share module names such as utils and network with GReMS.

docs.title: EnSplit
docs.text: ensplit_ddqn.py (agent), ensplit_env.py (environment) and train_ensplit.py reproduce the EnSplit DDQN: 128 neuron MLP, Huber loss, Adam with learning rate 1e-5, discount 0.9, 1500 episodes of 50 steps. The released agent is in checkpoints/ensplit/. By default the evaluator uses the brute force variant, which is an upper bound on what the DDQN can reach. Pass --ensplit-checkpoint checkpoints/ensplit/ensplit_best.pt to evaluate the learned agent.

docs.title: Fair comparison notes
docs.text:
• Bandwidth: baselines are capped at DISNET_BW_CAP = 200 Mbit/s so that their link model covers the same range as the generated networks (DISNET_PAPER_BW_CAP = 15 reproduces the original DiSNet testbed setting).
  • Time limits: DiSNet and MoDNN use path enumeration that is exponential in graph size. Evaluations of networks above 10 nodes use a shorter per step time limit. If a baseline times out repeatedly on a network, it is skipped for that network (the log says so).

docs.title: Latency model
docs.text: Latency is not measured on real hardware during training. It is computed by run_rl_live.py (function measure_rl_plan_latency_ms) from lookup tables, which makes millions of episodes affordable and makes all methods comparable.

docs.title: Ingredients
docs.text:
• Per layer compute time LAYER_IOT_FWD_MS (in config.py). Layer times were profiled on a Xeon E5-2690 and scaled so that the full VGG-16 pass takes 7253 ms, the Jetson Nano MAXN figure from the DiSNet paper.
  • Node speed. The compute time of a layer slice is LAYER_IOT_FWD_MS[l] * fraction / speedup(w) * slowdown, with speedup(w) = 1 + 0.4 * (w - 1) and slowdown = min(1 / (1 - rho), 4) where rho is the current MMPP background load of the node.
  • Transfers. bytes / (bandwidth_MBps * 1024^2) * 1000 ms plus per transfer overhead (OVERHEAD_PER_DATA_TRANSFER = 0.5 ms). If two nodes are not directly connected, the transfer is routed along the Dijkstra shortest path (store and forward).
  • Overheads. 5 ms per remote worker setup and 1.5 ms per chunk (OVERHEAD_REMOTE_NODE_SETUP, OVERHEAD_PER_CHUNK).
  • Receptive field overlap. A worker that processes a slice of a convolutional stage needs extra input rows from its neighbours. group_fov_overlap in config.py computes how many.

docs.title: Recursive worker to worker model
docs.text:
The communication model follows the paper section on the latency model. Each worker w of group g finishes at

Delta[g, w] = delta_C[w] + max over u in W[g-1, w] of ( Delta[g-1, u] + delta_comm[u, w] )

where W[g-1, w] is the set of workers of the previous group whose output rows w needs, delta_C is the compute time of w for its slice and delta_comm the transfer time from u to w. This yields a dependency DAG over workers. The end to end latency is the finish time of the last group, plus the transfer of the final activation to the node that runs the fully connected layers.

  • Hub to group 0 workers: input rows plus overlap, once per request.
  • Group g to group g + 1: every worker sends exactly the rows each consumer needs, over a direct link or a multi hop route.
  • Final spatial group to the FC node: the full activation. Fully connected layers run on one agent chosen node without horizontal split.

Version note

The latency model was revised shortly before the release (commit "Updated Latency Model", September 2026). Checkpoints trained with the older bottleneck model are not comparable and are not included.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The model is analytical. It captures compute, bandwidth, routing and overlap, but not packet loss, queueing inside the network, or memory contention beyond the penalty term. See Extending GReMS for how to plug in a different latency estimator.

docs.title: What is being optimised
docs.text:
A VGG-16 model with 21 layers (13 convolution, 5 max pool, 3 fully connected, input 224 x 224 x 3) must run inference on a wireless network of IoT devices. No single device is fast enough, so the model is split over several devices. GReMS produces a split plan for each request:

Decision Meaning Vertical split The 21 layers are cut into 1 to 6 consecutive groups (pipeline stages). Horizontal split Inside one spatial group the feature map is cut into chunks that run on parallel workers. Neighbouring chunks exchange the overlap rows that convolutions need. Hub The node that receives the input, distributes it to the first group and aggregates. Assignment Which physical node fills each worker slot of each group.

The metric is end to end latency in milliseconds, estimated with an analytical model (Latency model).

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
• Topologies are connected graphs with 3 to 20 nodes from four generator families: random geometric graph (RGG, used for training), Barabasi-Albert (BA), Watts-Strogatz (WS) and Erdos-Renyi (ER). BA, WS and ER are used to test generalisation.
  • Node capability is a weight in [1, 10] relative to a Jetson Nano in MAXN mode. A node of weight w runs layer l in LAYER_IOT_FWD_MS[l] / speedup(w) milliseconds with speedup(w) = 1 + 0.4 * (w - 1), a deliberately diminishing return (see DEVICE_SCALING_DIMINISHING_RETURN).
  • Link bandwidth: the base bandwidth of every edge is drawn log uniformly between 5 and 200 Mbit/s.
  • Topology files are pickled NetworkX graphs named varnet_<N>nodes[_<tag>]_<i>.txt. Test networks carry the tag test.

docs.title: Channel dynamics
docs.text:
Two Markov models make the conditions change over time. Both advance once per episode at env.reset(), so a channel state stays fixed during the steps of an episode. This lets the critic predict the whole discounted return from the first observation.

Compute load, two state MMPP per node (ComputeLoadModel)

State Background utilisation rho Transition LOW uniform 0.10 to 0.35 LOW to HIGH with probability 0.05 HIGH uniform 0.55 to 0.80 HIGH to LOW with probability 0.20

The compute time of a node is multiplied by an M/M/1 style slowdown min(1 / (1 - rho), 4).

Link bandwidth, two state Gilbert-Elliott per link (LinkBWModel)

State Bandwidth factor Transition (paper setting) GOOD 0.80 to 1.00 of base GOOD to BAD with probability 0.15 BAD 0.15 to 0.25 of base BAD to GOOD with probability 0.40

During evaluation the chains advance at every step of a 50 step trajectory, and all methods are scored on the same sequence of states.

docs.title: Episodes in training
docs.text: SplitEnv.reset() samples a network from the training pool, advances both chains and returns the first observation. An episode lasts EPISODE_LENGTH = 10 steps. At each step the agent proposes a plan for the same channel state and receives the reward. The previous action is part of the next observation.

docs.title: Train and test protocol
docs.text: Item Value Training topologies RGG, 50 networks per size Stage 1 sizes N = 4 to 10 Stage 2 sizes N = 4 to 20, sizes 11 to 20 sampled with twice the weight Test topologies 10 held out networks per size, never used in training Evaluation sizes 3 to 20 (size 3 was never trained on in either stage) Out of family tests WS, ER, BA with the same sizes, plus BA with m = 1, 3, 4

docs.title: Reward
docs.text:
reward = -ALPHA * log(latency_ms)          # ALPHA = 5.0, latency floored at 1 ms

The logarithm compresses latencies from about 100 ms to 100 000 ms into a stable signal. Shaped terms are added in environment.py:

Term Value Purpose Connectivity penalty per disconnected hub to worker pair, ramps from 5 to 50 over 500k steps forces plans that use existing links Weak link penalty beta 10, link below 2 MB/s but not zero avoids nearly dead first hop links Single node plan flat 140 keeps "everything on the hub" dominated by real splits Memory overload up to 200, scales with layers above NUM_LAYERS / ceil(sqrt(N)) pushes towards more stages on small networks Routing quality bonus up to +5, fraction of inter stage transfers on GOOD links low variance signal for link awareness Node utilisation bonus up to +25 by default, 0 for the released models disabled with NODE_UTIL_BONUS=0.0 because it destabilised fine tuning

Rewards are normalised online with a running mean and variance (Welford, RunningMeanStd) before the advantage computation, so the critic target stays near zero mean and unit variance when the channel regime shifts.

docs.title: PPO
docs.text: Parameter Stage 1 Stage 2 Algorithm PPO with GAE, discount 0.99, lambda 0.95 same Learning rate 3e-4, linear decay to 0 3e-5, linear decay to 0 Rollout and batch size 512 and 512 512 and 512 Epochs per update 4 4 Clip epsilon 0.2 0.2 Entropy coefficient 0.02, decays to 0.002 over 2M steps same Value coefficient 0.5 0.5 Gradient clipping 0.5 0.5 Timesteps 30 000 000 from scratch 10 000 000 from Stage 1 grems_final.pt Sizes N = 4 to 10 N = 4 to 20, sizes 11 and above with weight 2 CONN_PENALTY_START 5 (default) 50 (already converged)

docs.title: Why two stages
docs.text: Training from scratch on all sizes up to 20 is slow because large graphs are expensive to simulate and have a much larger action space. Stage 1 learns the core behaviour on small networks. Stage 2 exposes the converged policy to larger graphs at a low learning rate so it extends without forgetting. Several other fine tuning variants (node bonus on, small learning rate only, different penalty schedules) were explored during development. They destabilised the converged policy, which is why Stage 2 pins the connectivity penalty and disables the node bonus.

docs.title: Logging and checkpoints
docs.text:
• Console and logs/train_GReMS.log show reward, latency and PPO statistics every --log-interval rollouts.
  • Every --eval-interval steps the policy is evaluated on a fixed set of held out networks, and a row step, seen_lat_ms_all, seen_lat_ms_<topology> is appended to learning_curve.csv next to the checkpoints.
  • grems_best.pt is the best checkpoint by that evaluation, grems_final.pt the last one, grems_latest.pt a crash recovery snapshot every 50 rollouts.
  • Weights & Biases is optional. Pass --wandb-project <name> to enable it.
